questions.source_name: Grade9 authored Physics practice: Mechanics transfer
questions.stem: Two identical carts, each of mass m, are on a horizontal track. One cart moves at 8 m/s and collides head-on with the other cart initially at rest. They lock together. During the short collision, neglect the impulse of track friction. Afterwards, the joined carts slide on a rough horizontal section with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s². What distance do they travel after collision before stopping?
steps: 1. System and conservation choice: Over the short impact, horizontal external impulse is negligible. Horizontal momentum is conserved, but mechanical energy is not conserved because the carts stick.
2. Collision model: m(8) + m(0) = (2m)V gives V = 4 m/s immediately after impact.
3. After-collision braking: Kinetic-friction force is μ(2m)g, so deceleration a = μg = 2.5 m/s². Work–energy or v² = 2aL gives L = 4²/(2×2.5) = 3.2 m.
questions.check: Independent energy check: kinetic energy immediately after collision is (1/2)(2m)(4²) = 16m joules; friction does (0.25)(2m)(10)(3.2) = 16m joules of negative work. Initial kinetic energy was 32m joules; half was dissipated during sticking. Limits: as μ → 0⁺ the stopping distance diverges; doubling μ halves L. This is not an official examination question.

questions.source_name: Fluid Mechanics — Buoyancy in Accelerating Frames
questions.batch: Buoyant tension & relative acceleration in an elevator
questions.stem:
A solid block of density $\rho_s = 600\text{ kg/m}^3$ and mass $m = 3.0\text{ kg}$ is tied to the bottom of a container filled with water ($\rho_w = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$) by a light inextensible cord. The entire container is placed inside an elevator accelerating vertically upwards with constant acceleration $a = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$. Taking $g = 10.0\text{ m/s}^2$:

Determine the tension $T$ in the cord during upward acceleration, and the initial upward acceleration $a_{\text{rel}}$ of the block relative to the container immediately after the cord is severed.
steps: 1. In the upward accelerating elevator frame, effective gravity is g_eff = g + a = 10.0 + 2.0 = 12.0 m/s².
2. Block volume V = m / ρ_s = 3.0 / 600 = 0.0050 m³. Buoyant force F_B = ρ_w * V * g_eff = 1000 * 0.0050 * 12.0 = 60.0 N.
3. Effective weight W_eff = m * g_eff = 3.0 * 12.0 = 36.0 N.
4. Equilibrium gives tension T = F_B - W_eff = 60.0 - 36.0 = 24.0 N.
5. Immediately after cord is cut, net upward force F_net = 24.0 N; relative acceleration a_rel = F_net / m = 24.0 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s².
questions.check: Limiting check: as elevator acceleration a -> -g (free fall), g_eff -> 0, giving T = 0 N and a_rel = 0 m/s².

questions.source_name: Fluid Mechanics — Droplet Coalescence & Surface Energy Release
questions.batch: Non-linear geometric scaling & surface energy release
questions.stem:
1000 identical spherical water droplets, each of radius $r = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}$, coalesce into a single spherical drop. The surface tension of water is $T = 0.075\text{ N/m}$.

Calculate the net decrease in total surface area and the surface energy released during coalescence.
steps: 4. Area reduction ΔA = A_i - A_f = 3600πr² = 3.6π × 10⁻⁵ m² ≈ 1.131 × 10⁻⁴ m².
5. Released surface energy ΔU = T * ΔA = 0.075 * 1.131 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 8.48 × 10⁻⁶ J.
questions.check: Limiting fraction: ΔU / U_i = 1 - N^(-1/3) = 1 - 0.1 = 90% of surface energy released.
